issues.label: Standard of review for RAD's IFA determination
Standard of review for procedural fairness issue
Whether RAD erred in its IFA analysis (first prong: risk of persecution or danger)
Whether RAD erred in its IFA analysis (second prong: reasonableness of IFA)
Whether RAD breached procedural fairness by failing to warn Ms. Ambroise at outset of hearing that IFA would be raised

result.overall: The Court dismissed the judicial review application, finding the Refugee Appeal Division's decision reasonable on both prongs of the internal flight alternative test and no breach of procedural fairness regarding notice of the IFA issue.

themes.name: Internal Flight Alternative (IFA) Test
themes.summary: The Court analyzed the two-prong IFA test: risk of persecution or danger in the IFA and the reasonableness of the IFA for the claimant.

themes.name: Procedural Fairness and Notice of IFA
themes.summary: The Court considered whether the Refugee Protection Division breached procedural fairness by not warning the claimant at the outset that an IFA would be raised.

themes.name: Standard of Review
themes.summary: The Court discussed the applicable standards of review for the RAD's IFA determination and procedural fairness issues.

themes.name: Risk of Sexual Violence and State Protection
themes.summary: The Court examined the claimant's arguments about the risk of sexual violence in Haiti and the RAD's consideration of state protection.

arguments.quote: Ms. Ambroise alleges that the RAD erred in its analysis of the two-prong IFA test.
arguments.claim: The RAD incorrectly analyzed both the risk of persecution/danger and the reasonableness of the IFA.
arguments.outcome_note: The Court found the RAD's analysis reasonable on both prongs.

arguments.quote: She also argues that the RAD’s decision breached procedural fairness because the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) member failed to state at the outset of the hearing that an IFA would be raised.
arguments.claim: The RPD breached procedural fairness by not warning about the IFA issue at the hearing's start.
arguments.outcome_note: The Court found no breach as the claimant was informed during the hearing and had opportunity to respond.

arguments.quote: The parties agree that this issue must be reviewed on a standard of reasonableness.
arguments.claim: The RAD's IFA determination should be reviewed on a reasonableness standard.
arguments.authority: Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65

arguments.quote: The parties also agree that the second issue, that of procedural fairness, must be reviewed on a standard of correctness.
arguments.claim: Procedural fairness issues are reviewed on a correctness standard.
arguments.authority: Alkhoury v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 153

arguments.quote: Ms. Ambroise alleges that the RAD erred by failing to analyze the lack of state protection in Haiti.
arguments.claim: The RAD should have analyzed the effectiveness of state protection before concluding there was an IFA.
arguments.outcome_note: The Court held the RAD was not required to analyze state protection because it found no serious possibility of persecution.

arguments.quote: Ms. Ambroise further argues that the RAD’s decision is unreasonable given the evidence of conditions in Haiti, including sexual violence and criminal impunity.
arguments.claim: The RAD's decision was unreasonable given the evidence of sexual violence and impunity in Haiti.
arguments.outcome_note: The Court found the RAD's analysis reasonable and consistent with case law.

arguments.quote: Ms. Ambroise’s other arguments are that the RAD erred in its assessment of the documentary evidence and in its conclusion that Ms. Ambroise failed to demonstrate that she faces a serious possibility of persecution.
arguments.claim: The RAD erred in assessing evidence and concluding no serious possibility of persecution.
arguments.outcome_note: The Court found these arguments amounted to reweighing evidence, which is not its role.

arguments.quote: Ms. Ambroise also disputed the RAD’s conclusion that her attackers in Port-au-Prince did not have the ability or interest to look for her in Cap-Haïtien.
arguments.claim: The RAD unreasonably concluded the attackers would not pursue her in Cap-Haïtien.
arguments.outcome_note: The Court found no evidence of pursuit and upheld the RAD's conclusion.
arguments.authority: Dominguez Bando v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 FC 980

arguments.quote: Ms. Ambroise alleges that the RAD’s conclusion is unreasonable given the case law stating that the inability to find employment in one’s field of work in an IFA “may or may not make the IFA unreasonable”.
arguments.claim: The RAD unreasonably concluded the IFA was reasonable despite her inability to find nursing work.
arguments.outcome_note: The Court held the burden is high and the RAD's conclusion was reasonable.
arguments.authority: Mchedlishvilli v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2010 FC 630

arguments.quote: Ms. Ambroise states that this was a breach of procedural fairness.
arguments.claim: The RPD breached procedural fairness by not raising the IFA at the outset of the hearing.
arguments.outcome_note: The Court found the claimant was informed during the hearing and had opportunity to respond, so no breach occurred.
arguments.gap: Did not request leave to present further evidence or submissions after hearing.

holdings.quote: The RAD’s analysis of the danger or risk that Ms. Ambroise would face in the identified IFA ... were reasonable on the basis of the submissions raised by Ms. Ambroise.
holdings.statement: The RAD's decision on the risk of persecution or danger in the IFA was reasonable.

holdings.quote: it was reasonable for the RAD to conclude that Ms. Ambroise failed to meet the high threshold for establishing that the identified IFA is unreasonable.
holdings.statement: The RAD's conclusion that the IFA was reasonable was justified.

holdings.quote: there was no breach of procedural fairness.
holdings.statement: No procedural fairness breach occurred despite the IFA not being raised at the hearing's outset.

holdings.quote: The application for judicial review is dismissed.
holdings.statement: The judicial review application is dismissed.

holdings.quote: The parties agree that this issue must be reviewed on a standard of reasonableness.
holdings.statement: The RAD's IFA determination is reviewed on a reasonableness standard.

holdings.quote: the second issue, that of procedural fairness, must be reviewed on a standard of correctness.
holdings.statement: Procedural fairness issues are reviewed on a correctness standard.

holdings.quote: procedural fairness does not require that an IFA be raised at the outset of the hearing, although it is preferable to do so as early as possible.
holdings.statement: The duty of procedural fairness is met if the claimant has a reasonable opportunity to respond to the IFA issue, even if raised during the hearing.

holdings.quote: The threshold for the second prong of the IFA test is high, and the applicant must establish “actual and concrete evidence” of conditions that “would jeopardize the life and safety” of a claimant attempting to relocate temporarily to a safe area.
holdings.statement: To rebut the reasonableness of an IFA, the claimant must show actual and concrete evidence jeopardizing life or safety.

holdings.quote: The concept of an IFA is inherent to the definition of a Convention refugee under section 96 of the IRPA.
holdings.statement: A refugee claimant must seek safety within their country if a viable IFA exists.

holdings.quote: To rebut the viability of an identified IFA, a claimant must satisfy the RAD, on a balance of probabilities, that (1) the claimant will be subject to persecution ... and (2) conditions in the IFA are such that it would be unreasonable for the claimant to seek refuge there.
holdings.statement: The two-prong IFA test requires showing risk of persecution/danger and unreasonableness of the IFA.
holdings.quote_snapped: [13] To rebut the viability of an identified IFA, a claimant must satisfy the RAD, on a balance of probabilities, that (1) the claimant will be subject to persecution (on a “serious possibility” standard), or a section 97 danger or risk (on a “more likely than not” standard) in the proposed IFA;

rebuttals.quote: Ms. Ambroise alleges that the RAD erred by failing to analyze the lack of state protection in Haiti.
rebuttals.point: The RAD failed to analyze state protection effectiveness before concluding there was an IFA.
rebuttals.court_answer: The RAD was not required to analyze state protection because it found no serious possibility of persecution.

rebuttals.quote: Ms. Ambroise’s other arguments are that the RAD erred in its assessment of the documentary evidence and in its conclusion that Ms. Ambroise failed to demonstrate that she faces a serious possibility of persecution.
rebuttals.point: The RAD erred in assessing evidence and concluding no serious possibility of persecution.
rebuttals.court_answer: These arguments amount to reweighing evidence, which is not the Court's role in reasonableness review.

rebuttals.quote: Ms. Ambroise also disputed the RAD’s conclusion that her attackers in Port-au-Prince did not have the ability or interest to look for her in Cap-Haïtien.
rebuttals.point: The RAD unreasonably concluded the attackers would not pursue her in Cap-Haïtien.
rebuttals.court_answer: No evidence showed pursuit; the RAD's conclusion was reasonable.

rebuttals.quote: Ms. Ambroise states that this was a breach of procedural fairness.
rebuttals.point: The RPD breached procedural fairness by not raising the IFA at the outset of the hearing.
rebuttals.court_answer: The claimant was informed during the hearing and had opportunity to respond; no breach occurred.

authorities.quote: In Ward, the Supreme Court states that having established that the claimant has a fear, a panel is entitled to presume that persecution will be likely and the fear well-founded if there is an absence of state protection.
authorities.why: Clarifies when state protection analysis is required.
